title: Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively

paper.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex , a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery ( RSD ) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success–failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning ( ReSFT ) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex . Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents’ robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training.

(a) Prior environments assume clean tool feedback, whereas (b) real ones return noisy observations and user corrections at arbitrary turns. (d) Share of the eight tool-error families mined from 24,510 real error returns. 1 Introduction Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have extended their applications from natural language tasks to practical workflows that require long-horizon reasoning ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Barres et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . Meeting this demand requires agents not only to master tool interfaces but also to accumulate transferable interaction experience from dynamic environments. Building diverse, stateful environments that faithfully capture real-world interaction logic has therefore become the foundation for scaling agent capability. Recent studies to scale agent training environments can be roughly categorized into two groups. One group, exemplified by Simia ( Li et al., 2025 ) and GenEnv ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , treats LLMs as implicit textual world models that generate feedback from tool specifications and interaction histories. These approaches substantially reduce environmental engineering costs, but the feedback generated can be hallucinated. Instead, a complementary family explicitly reproduces real interaction logic, synthesizing executable tools and environment databases: it extracts databases from real-world service themes, generates executable tools, and synthesizes tasks with verifiable results ( Song et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Tu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026a ) . As a result, these executable environments give agents a basis for learning interaction patterns that transfer across environments. Although environment scaling improves interaction diversity and out-of-distribution generalization, existing agent-training paradigms still rely on an idealized assumption: agents interact with stable, well-controlled environments under minimal user intervention. This mismatch with real-world deployment reveals two inherent challenges (as shown in Figure 1 ): (1) Lack of noisy feedback. Real-world tool services are unreliable, frequently returning timeouts and service errors. Existing training environments usually assume stable and noise-free feedback, leaving agents underprepared for failure detection and recovery ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Gupta, 2026 ) . (2) Lack of user-guided correction. Real users actively intervene when an agent deviates from their intent, correcting its reasoning and actions. Existing user simulators often rely on standardized templates, with limited coverage of corrective instructions and diverse interaction styles during execution ( Barres et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Suhr and Artzi, 2023 ) . Together, these challenges reveal that agents still lack proactive reflection under noisy external feedback. Ideally, a robust agent should continuously perceive environmental noise, task failures, and user correction intent, then promptly revise its actions. Existing reflection methods explore inference-time reflection, correction-trajectory learning, and noise-augmented training ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , but most are trained in stateless or simplified environments, leaving one question open: How can we elicit proactive reflective capability in agents from execution failures in real-world environments? To address this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex , a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflective thinking in agents. It models reflection as a learnable meta-skill: transferable meta-skills are explicitly mined from execution failures and progressively internalized into the policy through verifiable reflection learning. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three components: (1) Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD). We anchor 557 high-usage real-world environment themes and automatically construct database-backed executable environments and tasks, injecting diverse tool-return failures to emulate noisy conditions. From a diverse LLM agent pool, we sample trajectories covering varied task types and response styles, and matched success/failure pairs are then mined into 1,170 reflection meta-skills across 557 environments. (2) Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT). Given the skill library, we design three auxiliary and verifiable reflection sampling strategies: Self-Reflection (SR), Skill Recovery (KR), and User-Centric Reflection (UR), which strengthen reflection at different levels. Supervised fine-tuning then internalizes these explicit skills into the agent policy. (3) On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO). To further elicit proactive reflection, ORPO combines Noisy Agent RL with reflection-guided on-policy distillation. For each task we match its environment’s reflection meta-skill and rollout in the noisy environment, optimizing the policy by reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. The same action tokens are then re-scored under a privileged skill context, and a confidence-weighted OPD objective ( Wu et al., 2026 ) turns this contrast into dense supervision for reflection decisions. Experiments on six long-horizon tool-use and noisy-interaction benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex . Further analysis shows that it improves noise robustness and keeps training dynamics stable, supporting scalable general-agent training. Therefore, our contributions are threefold: • We identify two gaps between idealized synthetic environments and real-world deployment in agent interaction, namely lack of noisy environment feedback and lack of user-guided correction during execution , highlighting the importance of reflection learning for noisy interactions. • We introduce RSD , which systematically builds a scalable noisy-environment ecosystem by incorporating real-tool perturbations and mining reflection meta-skills from large-scale success/ failure trajectory pairs sampled by an LLM Agent Pool. • We further propose ReSFT and ORPO. ReSFT builds multi-level reflection data through three sampling strategies and internalizes it by supervised fine-tuning; ORPO adds reflection-guided on-policy distillation to Noisy Agent RL for token-level supervision of failed executions. 2 Related Work Agent Reflection Learning. Agent reflection differs in where the corrective signal lives. Inference-time methods leave parameters untouched: Reflexion and Self-Refine append a verbal self-critique, and ExpeL retrieves cross-task insights at test time ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Because the critique comes from the policy that failed, a well-formed but wrong tool return is rarely contradicted. Training-time methods move the signal into a per-trajectory repair: Agent-R, ReflectRL, and LoongReflect learn from that repair ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and NoisyAgent exposes the policy to perturbed interaction under only a scalar return ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Either way, nothing accumulates into an environment-level statement a later episode can reuse. Agent-Reflex mines cross-model success/failure contrasts under the same injected noise into environment-indexed meta-skills and internalizes them through two-stage training. Scalable Environment Synthesis for Agent Training. Diverse, stateful environments underpin tool use and long-horizon decision making. One line of work simulates interaction feedback with language models, treating tool specifications and dialogue history as an implicit world model ( Li et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . A second makes the environment itself executable: EnvScaler and ScaleEnv synthesize tools with verifiable tasks ( Song et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ) , Agent-World scales database-backed services over hundreds of real-world themes and verifies outcomes through state transitions ( Dong et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , and EnvACE internalizes environment dynamics through world rehearsal ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . All of them scale the supply of solvable environments, whereas Agent-Reflex keeps the database-backed paradigm but turns the failures inside those environments into supervision, mining diagnosis and recovery rules from cross-model success/failure contrasts under perturbations derived from real tool errors.
